meta.title: Teaching Activities & Techniques
meta.randomizationRule: Randomize question selection/order and answer-option order on every attempt; never reuse an exact attempt signature.
meta.alignment: TKT Module 1 — Background to language teaching: types of activities and tasks for language and skills development
meta.scopeNote: Lesson frameworks and named approaches such as PPP, TBL, Test-Teach-Test, TPR, Guided Discovery, Grammar-Translation and Lexical Approach are reserved mainly for Unit 14.

questions.prompt: The teacher says a sentence and the whole class repeats it together. What is this?
questions.explanation: In a choral drill, learners repeat the model together as a class.

questions.prompt: The teacher says a phrase and one learner repeats it. What is this?
questions.explanation: In an individual drill, one learner repeats the teacher's model.

questions.prompt: The teacher says, “I bought a book. Pen.” Learners respond, “I bought a pen.” What type of drill is this?
questions.explanation: A substitution drill keeps the structure but replaces one item.

questions.prompt: The teacher says, “I went to the cinema. Didn't.” Learners respond, “I didn't go to the cinema.” What type of drill is this?
questions.explanation: A transformation drill requires learners to change the grammatical structure.

questions.prompt: What is the teacher doing when saying the target language clearly before learners repeat it?
questions.explanation: A model provides an example of the language learners are expected to repeat or use.

questions.prompt: Which activity gives the most controlled oral practice?
questions.explanation: The language pattern is tightly controlled and learners have little choice.

questions.prompt: Which term refers to the language the teacher provides for learners to imitate?
questions.explanation: A model is an example learners can repeat or use as a reference.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of drilling?
questions.explanation: Drilling gives learners repeated, guided practice of forms or pronunciation.

questions.prompt: Which drill changes affirmative sentences into negatives?
questions.explanation: The learner transforms one grammatical structure into another.

questions.prompt: Which statement about drilling is most accurate?
options: It can support accurate production but usually offers limited communicative choice
It always develops reading for gist
questions.correctAnswer: It can support accurate production but usually offers limited communicative choice
questions.explanation: Drills are generally controlled and focus on accurate production.

questions.prompt: The teacher shows a picture of a carrot and asks, “What's this?” because learners may know the word. What technique is this?
questions.explanation: Eliciting uses questions or clues to get learners to supply language or information.

questions.prompt: A learner cannot remember a word, so the teacher gives the first sound. What technique is this?
questions.explanation: A prompt gives a clue to help a learner remember or produce language.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between eliciting and simply telling?
options: Eliciting gets learners to provide information themselves
questions.correctAnswer: Eliciting gets learners to provide information themselves
questions.explanation: The teacher uses questions or clues instead of immediately giving the answer.

questions.prompt: Which teacher move is a prompt?
options: Give the first word of a phrase to help a learner continue
Ask learners to repeat a sentence together
questions.correctAnswer: Give the first word of a phrase to help a learner continue
questions.explanation: A prompt provides partial support to help retrieval.

questions.prompt: Why can eliciting be useful?
options: It activates learners' existing knowledge and increases participation
It guarantees all learners know the answer
It removes the need for teaching
questions.correctAnswer: It activates learners' existing knowledge and increases participation
questions.explanation: Eliciting reveals what learners know and involves them actively.

questions.prompt: The teacher asks targeted questions to get learners to produce the past tense of a familiar verb. What is this?
questions.explanation: The teacher is drawing known language from learners.

questions.prompt: The teacher says, “It begins with /b/...” to help a learner remember “borrow”. What is this?
questions.explanation: The teacher gives a clue rather than the complete answer.

questions.prompt: Which statement about prompting is correct?
options: It gives support while leaving learners some responsibility for producing the answer
It always supplies the entire answer
It is another term for final assessment
questions.correctAnswer: It gives support while leaving learners some responsibility for producing the answer
questions.explanation: Prompts scaffold learner retrieval without fully taking over.

questions.prompt: Which activity most clearly uses elicitation?
options: Ask learners what vocabulary they already know about transport
Give learners a finished list to copy
Play a recording with no response
questions.correctAnswer: Ask learners what vocabulary they already know about transport
questions.explanation: The teacher is drawing information from learners.

questions.prompt: Which teacher action is least likely to develop learner participation?
options: Immediately provide every answer before learners have a chance to respond
Use clues to elicit known language
Prompt a learner who is nearly able to answer
questions.correctAnswer: Immediately provide every answer before learners have a chance to respond
questions.explanation: Eliciting and prompting encourage learners to contribute rather than remain passive.

questions.prompt: Learners complete sentences using one target structure with only one possible answer. What type of practice is this?
questions.explanation: Controlled practice limits learner choice so attention can stay on accurate use of the target language.

questions.prompt: Learners discuss their opinions using any language they need. What type of practice is this?
questions.explanation: Free practice gives learners substantial choice over the language they use.

questions.prompt: A survey requires learners to use “Have you ever...?” but allows them to create their own follow-up questions. What is this likely to be?
questions.explanation: The target structure is guided, but learners still have some choice.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between controlled and free practice?
options: The amount of choice learners have in the language they use
Whether the teacher uses a board
questions.correctAnswer: The amount of choice learners have in the language they use
questions.explanation: Control refers to how tightly the language output is predetermined.

questions.prompt: Why might a lesson move from controlled to less controlled to freer practice?
options: To gradually increase learner independence in using the target language
questions.correctAnswer: To gradually increase learner independence in using the target language
questions.explanation: A progression can support accuracy first and then more independent use.

questions.prompt: Which task is most controlled?
options: Substitute one word in a fixed sentence pattern
Role-play a complaint using any appropriate language
questions.correctAnswer: Substitute one word in a fixed sentence pattern
questions.explanation: The output is almost completely predetermined.

questions.prompt: Which task is most likely to develop fluency?
questions.explanation: Freer practice allows learners to prioritise communicating meaning with greater language choice.

questions.prompt: A task gives learners sentence starters but lets them finish the ideas themselves. What is this best described as?
questions.explanation: There is support and some constraint, but learners still make meaningful choices.

questions.prompt: Which statement is most accurate?
options: Controlled practice usually prioritises accuracy more than free practice
Free practice always has one correct sentence
Controlled practice gives maximum language choice
questions.correctAnswer: Controlled practice usually prioritises accuracy more than free practice
questions.explanation: Controlled tasks limit choice to help learners practise a target form accurately.

questions.prompt: Which sequencing principle is pedagogically sensible?
options: Move toward greater choice as learners become more secure with the target language
Begin with maximum complexity regardless of learner readiness
Keep all practice fully controlled forever
questions.correctAnswer: Move toward greater choice as learners become more secure with the target language
questions.explanation: Gradual release supports learners as they move toward independent production.

questions.prompt: A task asks learners to listen and choose the correct picture. What kind of task is this?
questions.explanation: The task develops or checks receptive understanding rather than requiring learners to produce extended language.

questions.prompt: A task asks learners to write a short email. What kind of task is this?
questions.explanation: Writing is a productive skill, so learners are producing language.

questions.prompt: Which skills are productive?
questions.explanation: Speaking and writing require learners to produce language.

questions.prompt: Which skills are receptive?
questions.explanation: Reading and listening involve processing incoming language.

questions.prompt: Why can the same activity type sometimes serve different purposes?
options: Its purpose depends on how the activity is designed and used
Every activity has only one possible purpose
Task purpose depends only on classroom size
questions.correctAnswer: Its purpose depends on how the activity is designed and used
questions.explanation: The same task format can focus on different skills or levels of control depending on design.

questions.prompt: A jigsaw listening task mainly develops:
questions.explanation: Learners first process spoken information, then share it with others.

questions.prompt: A guided writing task is primarily:
questions.explanation: Learners produce written language, although with support.

questions.prompt: Which activity primarily develops comprehension?
options: Read a text and identify the writer's main point
questions.correctAnswer: Read a text and identify the writer's main point
questions.explanation: The learner is processing meaning from written input.

questions.prompt: Which activity primarily develops productive speaking?
questions.explanation: A survey usually requires learners to ask and answer questions orally.

questions.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes comprehension and production tasks?
options: Comprehension tasks focus on understanding input; production tasks require learners to create language
questions.correctAnswer: Comprehension tasks focus on understanding input; production tasks require learners to create language
questions.explanation: The central distinction is receptive processing versus language production.

questions.prompt: Learners act as a hotel receptionist and a guest in a given situation. What task type is this?
questions.explanation: Role-play gives learners roles to act out in a situation.

questions.prompt: Learners ask classmates questions and record their answers. What task type is this?
questions.explanation: A survey involves gathering information from others through questions.

questions.prompt: Learners work together to decide which five items are most important for survival. What task type is this?
questions.explanation: Learners discuss, negotiate and put items into an order of importance.

questions.prompt: Two learners have different information and must communicate to complete the whole picture. What kind of task is this?
questions.explanation: Learners need to exchange missing information to complete the task.

questions.prompt: Why are problem-solving tasks communicative?
options: Learners exchange ideas and negotiate meaning to reach a solution
questions.correctAnswer: Learners exchange ideas and negotiate meaning to reach a solution
questions.explanation: The task creates a reason to communicate in order to solve a problem.

questions.prompt: Which task usually involves learners taking on roles in a simulated situation?
questions.explanation: Learners act within an assigned or imagined role.

questions.prompt: Learners quickly generate as many ideas as possible about a topic before writing. What activity is this?
questions.explanation: Brainstorming rapidly generates ideas, often as preparation for speaking or writing.

questions.prompt: A text is cut into sections; different learners read different sections and then share information. What is this?
questions.explanation: In a jigsaw task, different learners hold different parts of the information and must combine them.

questions.prompt: Learners put a set of sentences into the correct order to reconstruct a text. What is this?
questions.explanation: A jumbled-text task asks learners to restore the correct order of text parts.

questions.prompt: Which task most strongly requires negotiation and agreeing/disagreeing?
questions.explanation: Learners must discuss priorities and reach agreement about an ordered list.

questions.prompt: The teacher tells a learner, “Excellent work.” What teaching technique is this?
questions.explanation: Praise tells learners they have done well and can support confidence.

questions.prompt: Learners look again at language they studied last week in order to remember it better. What is this?
questions.explanation: Review means returning to previously taught language or skills.

questions.prompt: A learner says, “He don't like it.” The teacher repeats, “Don't?” with rising intonation. What correction technique is this?
questions.explanation: The teacher echoes the problematic part to encourage self-correction.

questions.prompt: Learners correct one another's mistakes during pair work. What is this?
questions.explanation: Peer correction occurs when learners help correct each other's language.

questions.prompt: Why might a teacher use a correction code in writing?
options: To help learners identify and correct their own errors
To give learners the complete rewritten answer
questions.correctAnswer: To help learners identify and correct their own errors
questions.explanation: Correction codes support learner awareness and self-correction.

questions.prompt: The teacher uses fingers to show where a learner's word-order error occurred. What technique is this?
questions.explanation: Finger correction visually locates the position of a spoken error.

questions.prompt: Which feedback technique gives learners responsibility for improving their own language?
options: Immediate teacher replacement of every answer
questions.explanation: Self-correction encourages learners to monitor and repair their own language.

questions.prompt: Which statement about praise is most accurate?
options: Specific, credible praise can support confidence and motivation
Praise should replace all corrective feedback
questions.correctAnswer: Specific, credible praise can support confidence and motivation
questions.explanation: Effective praise recognises successful performance and can encourage learners.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of review?
options: Strengthen memory of previously taught language or skills
questions.correctAnswer: Strengthen memory of previously taught language or skills
questions.explanation: Review revisits prior learning to help learners remember and consolidate it.

questions.prompt: Which teacher response best balances feedback and learner independence?
options: Give a clue and allow the learner to self-correct when possible
Correct every error before the learner can respond
questions.correctAnswer: Give a clue and allow the learner to self-correct when possible
questions.explanation: Prompts and self-correction can provide support while keeping learners actively involved.

matchingSets.instruction: Match each classroom action with the correct teaching term.

items.example: The whole class repeats the teacher's model.
The teacher asks targeted questions to get known language from learners.
The teacher gives the first sound to help a learner remember a word.
Learners use one target structure with very limited language choice.
Learners act out a situation using assigned roles.
Learners revisit language studied in an earlier lesson.

matchingSets.instruction: Match each activity with its main purpose or category.

items.example: Change an affirmative sentence into a negative one.
Use a target structure but create some of your own content.
Listen and choose the correct picture.
Different learners combine separate pieces of information.
Learners help correct one another's language.
